title: Signal engine orchestration
description: analyse() in app/signals/engine.py: pulls indicator outputs, evaluates Screens 1-3, applies the Impulse gate, computes confidence, and produces the final (signal, confidence, breakdown) per docs/Analyse.md §5.

checklist.step: Implement BUY rule: tide=BULLISH, impulse != RED, wave shows oversold pullback, trigger fired
Implement SELL rule: tide=BEARISH, impulse != GREEN, wave shows overbought rally, trigger fired
Default to HOLD when conditions are partial/conflicting/tide is NEUTRAL
Write unit tests covering each Screen 1/2/3 + Impulse combination explicitly (not just the happy BUY/SELL paths)
Run the verify-elder-signal skill/agent against this module once implemented, before considering it done
Run pytest --cov=app --cov-report=term-missing and confirm no regression

decisions.decision: docs/Analyse.md §5's BUY/SELL rules say the Wave condition 'shows/showed' an oversold pullback or overbought rally -- not just 'shows' -- acknowledging the pullback/rally can have already ended by the day the Trigger actually fires (the Trigger firing, close crossing back above/below the prior bar, is itself evidence the pullback/rally is over). Implemented this as a trailing lookback: `_wave_showed_state()` re-evaluates `evaluate_wave()` over each of the last 5 daily bars (today inclusive, holding today's Tide direction fixed across the window rather than recomputing Screen 1 per day) and treats a qualifying OVERSOLD_PULLBACK/OVERBOUGHT_RALLY on *any* of those bars as satisfying the Wave condition for BUY/SELL, not only a match on today's bar. The 5-day window is a new, undocumented constant (`_WAVE_LOOKBACK_DAYS`).
decisions.rationale: Without this, BUY/SELL would require the oversold/overbought oscillator state and the Trigger to both hold on the exact same bar -- but Stochastic %K (5,3,3) is a smoothed, several-bar-lagging read, so this coincidence is far from guaranteed and, empirically (see TestAnalyseEndToEnd's real end-to-end fixtures), a clean pullback-then-resumption sequence commonly has the oscillator already off its extreme by the day the Trigger fires. Requiring same-bar-only would silently make BUY/SELL rare-to-unreachable for exactly the textbook Elder setup the app exists to detect, contradicting §5's own 'shows/showed' wording. Rejected: (a) same-bar-only (literal reading of 'shows', ignoring 'showed') -- too restrictive per the above, and ignores half of the doc's own sentence; (b) tracking Wave state as separately-persisted history in a new DB/session concept -- unnecessary, since the full daily OHLCV history is already available in-memory on every `analyse()` call, so re-deriving 'did this happen recently' by re-slicing the existing DataFrame is simpler and needs no new persistence; (c) an unbounded lookback (any qualifying bar ever) -- rejected as it would let an arbitrarily stale pullback from months ago still justify a fresh BUY today, which isn't what 'showed' plausibly means in context. 5 trading days (~1 calendar week) was chosen as a defensible default width for how long a Wave setup stays 'live' before the Trigger should have already resolved it, with no doc-given number to anchor it to -- flagged, like screen2-wave's own spike-threshold decision, as a candidate for backtested tuning later (Analyse.md §10). The lookback recomputes `evaluate_wave()` per candidate day using the full history *up to* that day (not a right-truncated slice), so each day's oscillator/Force-Index warm-up is unaffected -- only the trailing window of *days checked* is bounded, not the history each check is computed from.

decisions.decision: The confidence breakdown's `oscillator_extremity` and `elder_ray_confirmation` components are always scored off *today's* bar (the bar the signal is emitted on), even when a BUY/SELL only fired because of the lookback 'showed' case above (i.e. the oscillator itself may have already left the extreme zone by today, scoring `oscillator_extremity` at 0.0 for a signal that's still a genuine, doc-compliant BUY/SELL).
decisions.rationale: Confidence-scoring's `score_oscillator_extremity()`/`score_elder_ray_confirmation()` (confidence-scoring task) are pure functions over the *latest* bar's data by design -- there is no 'as of which historical bar' parameter, and retrofitting one would mean threading a second, competing 'which day actually qualified' concept through the confidence layer purely for this one case. Scoring today's (possibly less extreme, or already-recovered) reading is also a defensible reading of confidence itself: a BUY that only qualifies via a several-day-old pullback is legitimately a weaker/staler setup than one where the oscillator is still at its extreme today, and a lower oscillator-extremity component score is a fair, not spurious, reflection of that -- the alternative (re-deriving the qualifying historical bar's own oscillator/Elder-Ray reading and scoring against that instead) would overstate confidence for a signal that's arguably less fresh. Rejected: extending `_wave_showed_state()` (or a new helper) to also return *which* bar qualified and threading that bar's own wave/bull_power/bear_power snapshot into the confidence components instead of today's -- adds real complexity (a second code path, a second set of tests) for a scoring nuance Analyse.md §6 doesn't ask for or even acknowledge (§6 is written entirely in terms of the signal's current oscillator/Elder-Ray state, with no notion of 'how it looked N days ago'). `volume_confirmation` and `impulse_gate`/`tide_alignment` are unaffected by this question -- §6 phrases volume_confirmation specifically as 'trigger bar volume', which is unambiguously today's bar regardless of when Wave qualified. See TestAnalyseEndToEnd's two real (unmocked) end-to-end tests for a concrete example: both the BUY and SELL fixtures deliberately construct a 'showed, not shows' scenario (asserting `result.screens['wave']['state'] != 'OVERSOLD_PULLBACK'`/`'OVERBOUGHT_RALLY'` on the signal-emitting bar) and confirm the signal still fires correctly with a full 5-component breakdown.

decisions.decision: A HOLD signal always returns `confidence=0`, `confidence_band='Low'`, and an empty `breakdown` list -- the five confidence components (`score_tide_alignment` etc.) are never called for HOLD.
decisions.rationale: Every one of the five component-scoring functions in `app.signals.confidence` takes a `signal_direction` argument constrained to `'BUY'`/`'SELL'` and raises `ValueError` otherwise (confidence-scoring task's own explicit design) -- there is no direction to score agreement *toward* when no fresh trade signal is being emitted at all, so computing a confidence score for HOLD would mean fabricating an implied direction. docs/Analyse.md §6 frames confidence entirely as 'how strongly the underlying indicators agree' with an (implicitly BUY-or-SELL) signal, never addressing what a HOLD's confidence should mean. Rejected: (a) picking whichever direction the Tide leans (e.g. BULLISH tide -> score against 'BUY' even though the actual signal is HOLD) and reporting that as HOLD's confidence -- this would present a confidence number for a trade the app isn't actually recommending, which is more misleading than informative, especially given §6's own explicit warning that confidence 'shouldn't be misread as a statistical guarantee'; a nonzero number on a HOLD invites exactly that misreading. (b) Some non-zero neutral placeholder (e.g. 50) -- arbitrary, and would misrepresent 'no evaluation performed' as 'a mediocre score was computed'. `confidence=0`/`'Low'`/`breakdown=[]` was chosen as the reading that doesn't fabricate a scored direction: 0/Low is the correctly-behaving floor of the documented 0-100/Low-Medium-High scale, and an empty breakdown is honest about no per-component scoring having actually run, rather than an empty list being mistaken for '0.0 on every component' if it were populated with zeros instead.

decisions.decision: `SignalResult` (app/signals/engine.py) was extended beyond the literal '(signal, confidence, breakdown)' tuple named in this task's own description and docs/architecture/Backend.md §5, to also carry `screens` (the docs/architecture/API.md `screens.{tide,impulse,wave,trigger}` shape) and `indicators` (`indicators.{ema_13,ema_26,macd_histogram,bull_power,bear_power}`), both populated unconditionally (regardless of `signal`).
decisions.rationale: The api-stocks-analysis task (depends_on this one) is described as 'fetch OHLCV via cache, call signals.engine.analyse(), map SignalResult to AnalysisResponse' -- and AnalysisResponse (app/api/schemas.py) requires `screens` and `indicators` alongside `signal`/`confidence`/`confidence_band`/`confidence_breakdown`. Without this, api-stocks-analysis's handler would need to independently re-call evaluate_tide/evaluate_impulse/evaluate_wave/evaluate_trigger and recompute EMA/MACD-Histogram/Elder-Ray itself just to fill in the rest of the response -- duplicating work analyse() already does internally and risking the API-layer's recomputation silently drifting from what actually drove the signal/confidence it's reporting alongside. Rejected: leaving SignalResult exactly as the pre-existing stub declared it (signal/confidence/confidence_band/breakdown only) and pushing screens/indicators construction entirely into the API layer -- narrower per the task's literal wording, but sets up exactly the duplication/drift risk above for the very next task in the dependency chain, and there's no other consumer of analyse() today that this broader return shape would burden. `indicators`/`screens` are always populated (not just for BUY/SELL) because they're informational context in the API response regardless of what signal fired -- an analyst viewing a HOLD ticker still wants to see the current EMA/MACD-Histogram/Elder-Ray/Tide/Wave/Trigger state, not just a bare 'HOLD'.

decisions.decision: Closed out docs/tasks/impulse-system.json's checklist item 4 ('Confirm signal-engine-orchestration actually enforces the gate') to done: true, with this note added there, since that task's own decisions array explicitly deferred verifying real gate enforcement to this task. `_determine_signal()` in app/signals/engine.py now requires `impulse != 'RED'` for a fresh BUY and `impulse != 'GREEN'` for a fresh SELL -- both a Red-gated would-be-BUY and a Green-gated would-be-SELL fall through to HOLD rather than being emitted, per docs/Analyse.md §3's 'do not emit a fresh Buy signal even if Screen 2/3 line up' / mirror-image Sell wording. Covered by dedicated regression tests (TestDetermineSignal::test_buy_blocked_by_red_impulse, test_sell_blocked_by_green_impulse; TestAnalyseCombinations::test_bullish_red_oversold_fired_is_hold_not_buy, test_bearish_green_overbought_fired_is_hold_not_sell) that assert a fully-aligned-otherwise setup still degrades to HOLD once the opposing-color gate is added.
decisions.rationale: Verified via re-reading impulse-system.json's decisions[1]/decisions[2]: the gate's *computation* (GREEN/RED/BLUE) was already correct and complete, but its *enforcement* was explicitly left unimplemented and unverified pending this task existing -- decisions[2] says 'This item should be revisited and closed out for real once signal-engine-orchestration exists and actually calls evaluate_impulse().' That is now true: analyse() calls evaluate_impulse() and _determine_signal() enforces the gate as described above, so the checklist item's literal wording ('confirm...enforces') can now be honestly marked done rather than left permanently false on a merged, closed task.

comments.summary: analyse() + _wave_showed_state() call evaluate_wave() up to 11 times per invocation (1 direct + up to 5 for each of the two lookback target states), each redoing the full Stochastic/Force-Index/rolling-std computation over its slice; one of the two lookback loops is guaranteed fully wasted since evaluate_wave can only return OVERSOLD_PULLBACK for a BULLISH tide or OVERBOUGHT_RALLY for a BEARISH tide, never both. Not a correctness issue at current data sizes, but a real reuse/efficiency gap worth closing (single pass over the lookback window, check both target states against one evaluate_wave call per slice). Non-blocking; filed as signal-engine-orchestration-followups.

evaluate_impulse() (app/signals/impulse.py, pre-existing) internally computes ema(daily_close, 13) and macd_histogram(daily_close) but discards the series, returning only the GREEN/RED/BLUE color. analyse() now separately recomputes ema(daily_close, 13) and macd_components(daily_close).histogram on the same daily_close for the new `indicators` dict -- identical values computed twice with no sharing. Correctness is unaffected (indicators doesn't depend on evaluate_impulse's return value), but it's real duplicated work this PR introduces now that engine.py needs those series for a second purpose. Non-blocking; filed as signal-engine-orchestration-followups.
